item.title: Conversation Partners: Application Open — Thu Sep 3, 5:00 PM — Online
item.description:
In our conversation partners program, you can practice a language one-on-one with a native speaker—and make a new friend!
We will match you with an IU Bloomington student or staff member who can help you learn a language that interests you, and who wants to learn your language. You and your partner will talk and write in both languages. Because your partner will be a native speaker, you will learn how to use the language in daily conversation. You will learn about each other’s culture, too. The matching process is based on the number of applicants and range of spoken languages.
You and your partner will meet at least once a week during the semester. You can meet whenever and wherever you want. Feel free to try out locations other than campus buildings, such as coffee shops, American or international restaurants, parks, or the IU Art Museum.

item.title: Singles | Soundtracks of a Generation — Thu Sep 3, 7:00 PM — Indiana University Cinema
item.description: Arranged as an episodic comedy, Singles spotlights the intertwined lives of the co-habitants, friends, and bandmates of the same Seattle apartment building. Foregrounded by the tumultuous romantic relationship between Steve (Campbell Scott) and Linda (Kyra Sedgwick)—who meet at an Alice in Chains concert, of course!—the drama extends to their friendship with Janet Livermore (Bridget Fonda), who is tirelessly trying to win the affection of grunge-rocker Cliff Poncier (Matt Dillon). as well as their neighbor Debbie Hunt (Sheila Kelly), who is aching for a husband who appreciates her and her fantastic earrings. The film also features an endless stream of stellar cameos, including Eric Stoltz, Bill Pullman, Tom Skerritt, Peter Horton, Tim Burton, Eddie Vedder, and so many more! item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment — Fri Sep 4 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers — Fri Sep 4 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence) Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. item.title: Home Away from Home: Student Life on Campus — Fri Sep 4, 9:00 AM — HERMAN B WELLS LIBRARY
item.description:
Spanning across four decades—1970s to the 2000s—items including scrapbooks, photographs, student papers, and handbooks demonstrate life on and off campus. From decorating dorm rooms to chasing campus ghosts, students have always found ways to build community and make new memories. This exhibit highlights the student experience and the multitude of ways students found a sense of home, identity and belonging at Indiana University.
Source: IU Bloomington Libraries

item.title: Asian Cultures Around Campus: Henna Fridays — Fri Sep 4, 2:30 PM — Asian Culture Center (807 E 10th street
item.description:
The term Mehendi is the Indian word for Henna, and it is also the term used to describe the art of applying henna. Come and learn the basic designs and application techniques of Henna or Mehendi, which is used to create temporary tattoos. Please feel free to bring your friends to learn more about Desi culture and the significance of Mehendi in the Indian culture! If you come with a group of more than 7 members, please email acc@iu.edu in advance so we can prepare the henna materials.
All Indiana University events, groups, activities, and educational, cultural, and historical observances welcome all IU students and other members of the Indiana University community.

item.title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature — Mon Sep 7 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment — Mon Sep 7 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers — Mon Sep 7 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence) Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. item.description:
